item.title: Centuries of child labor left lasting spinal damage in Dutch children, study finds
item.description: Children in the postmedieval Dutch workforce worked so hard that their spines became worn and deformed, with some children affected before they even had a chance to lose their baby teeth, a new study published in the International Journal of Paleopathology finds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chinese coastguard has 0.3% chance of using weapons in disputed waters, war game suggests
item.description: A Chinese coastguard ship is shielding a cluster of fishing boats when several small, fast vessels begin circling – sometimes darting closer, sometimes backing off. Are they just curious fishermen? Or are they probing for a weak spot, trying to lure the patrol ship into a trap? In the real world, a split-second decision could escalate a tense maritime stand-off into something far more dangerous. This is exactly the kind of nerve‑wracking scenario Chinese coastguard researchers have been running... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Keto diet cut liver fat by 67% in a clinical trial
item.description: A ketogenic diet outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in several measures of metabolic health during a clinical trial involving people with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease. All three groups lost about 10% of their body weight, but keto reduced liver fat by 67%, compared with 45% for the other diets. About half of the keto group also no longer qualified as having prediabetes after four to five months. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Corea del Sur está lista para lanzar un cohete que le fue prohibido durante casi 50 años
item.description: Los países con capacidad militar miran al espacio porque allí puede estar su mejor "espía", en forma de satélites propios e independientes. Y para eso antes hacen falta cohetes. En 1979, Corea del Sur vio capada esa posibilidad, pero hace apenas un lustro recuperó plena libertad para desarrollarlos y no ha perdido el tiempo: tras varias pruebas previas, ya se dispone a probar por primera vez la versión operativa completa de su cohete militar de combustible sólido. Un cohete largamente esperado . Su nombre es Mir (dragón, en coreano), un lanzador de combustible sólido de la Agency for Defense… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Dogs may hold surprising clues to human longevity
item.description: Dogs and humans may have more in common when it comes to aging than scientists realized. Researchers with the Dog Aging Project found that patterns of small molecules in dogs’ blood were linked to longer or shorter lifespans in remarkably similar ways to those seen in people. These metabolic “fingerprints” could offer clues about the biological processes that drive aging, including metabolism, inflammation, and cellular stress. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists turn one of the hardest plastics to recycle into high-performance engine lubricant
item.description: Researchers have discovered a way to turn notoriously difficult-to-recycle PVC plastic into a key ingredient used in high-performance lubricants such as engine oil. The technique could give mountains of plastic waste a valuable second life while making lubricant production more sustainable. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: 324-million-year-old insect still had swimming paddles
item.description: A remarkable fossil unearthed in Texas sheds light on the evolutionary journey of insects transitioning from aquatic to terrestrial life. This ancient species featured paddle-like limbs designed for swimming and additional legs on its abdomen, indicating a semi-aquatic lifestyle in shallow coastal regions. This find is crucial in understanding the slow, gradual adaptations insects underwent over millions of years in their evolutionary history. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Talking to your children about consent and sexual violence can be hard. Here's how to start the conversation
item.description: There have been multiple high-profile alleged incidents of sexual violence against women and girls in news headlines this month. Some involve teenage boys. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nano-sandwich photocathode improves solar conversion of CO₂ into ethanol
item.description: Czech researchers at Charles University in Prague, led by Pavla Eliášová, have developed an advanced photocathode that helps convert the greenhouse gas carbon dioxide into pure ethanol using sunlight. The new technology solves a long-standing problem of material degradation in water, achieves record conversion efficiency and opens the way toward sustainable production of green fuels. The paper is published in the journal Advanced Energy Materials. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The universe is still speeding up, but nobody knows why
item.description: A major new analysis challenges recent claims that the universe's expansion is slowing, finding that the evidence for cosmic acceleration remains strong. The findings preserve the leading role of dark energy, while leaving scientists with the enduring mystery of what this strange cosmic force actually is. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Long-term melatonin use linked to 90% higher heart failure risk
item.description: People with chronic insomnia who used melatonin long term had a roughly 90% higher risk of developing heart failure over five years, according to a large preliminary study. The findings do not prove melatonin causes heart problems, but they raise new questions about the safety of taking the popular sleep supplement for extended periods. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Australia’s red soil may be hiding a massive clean energy source
item.description: Researchers have discovered that Western Australia’s iron-rich rocks can naturally generate hydrogen and that the process may be boosted to produce much larger amounts. If it can be scaled up, the vast formations beneath the Pilbara could become a major new source of low-emission energy for Australia and potentially the world. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Viking woman’s clothes preserved by her jewellery for 1,300 years
item.description: Danish archaeologists discovered rare Viking textile remains near Varde. Corrosion from jewelry preserved these ancient wool and linen fragments. This discovery offers a rare glimpse into Viking dress from 1,300 years ago. Researchers will analyze the fibers and teeth for more information. Dating the textiles will reveal if ornaments were new or inherited. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: A wooden relic that survived the sack of Jerusalem's First Temple was unearthed by archaeologists, now they are finding shocking answers
item.description: In a remarkable find, archaeologists uncovered ancient wooden beams from the destruction of Jerusalem's First Temple, dating back over 2,600 years to 586 B.C. These preserved sycamore beams, covered in melted plaster, are believed to have supported the roof of an inner courtyard. By analyzing the growth rings, researchers have accurately dated this crucial archaeological evidence, providing an extraordinary link to Jerusalem's rich and ancient history. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

Statins are already commonly prescribed to people under the age of 75 who meet certain risk criteria, such as having diabetes and high cholesterol, to prevent them from having… Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: Your sleep may be hiding an early clue to Alzheimer’s
item.description: Frequent micro-awakenings during sleep were linked to higher genetic risk for Alzheimer’s in healthy middle-aged adults who had no symptoms. The discovery raises the possibility that subtle changes during sleep could offer an early warning signal years before memory problems appear. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover why damaged nerves struggle to heal
item.description: Scientists have identified a protein that acts like a brake on the nervous system’s ability to repair damaged connections. Blocking AHR helped injured nerve fibers regrow and improved movement and sensation in mice with nerve or spinal cord injuries. The discovery could eventually point toward new treatments designed to shift neurons from simply surviving an injury to actively rebuilding themselves. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Many cities buried urban streams. Here's how to bring them back
item.description: As many cities developed, streams that once flowed on the surface were buried underground to make way for growing infrastructure. However, as heavier rainfall, extreme weather and aging infrastructure place growing pressure on cities, these buried streams could become part of the solution. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rethinking bluegreen aphid control as insecticide resistance spreads
item.description: When an insecticide application fails to control bluegreen aphid, application conditions may not be the only cause. Research has identified resistant populations across southern Australia, confirming that repeated reliance on broad-spectrum insecticides is no longer sustainable. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How AI‑powered policing is endangering the public's trust in police
item.description: Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, artificial intelligence (AI) has dominated the cultural landscape. Uptake across various sectors, including law enforcement, quickly followed, usually with minimal foresight and little to no guardrails, like effective policies or laws, to govern AI use. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Climate policy could learn from people who already live within the limits of sufficiency
item.description: Tina Nyfors, who recently defended her doctoral thesis at the University of Helsinki, studied sufficiency, a way of living and a principle for organizing society to stay within environmental limits while ensuring that people have enough. Nyfors directs attention to people whose carbon footprint is already in line with sufficiency and refers to them as the sufficiency class. Their way of life has a moderate climate impact yet still meets their needs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The discovery of the Great Barrier Reef's whale maternity ward
item.description: It started with a simple message: "This is the year to do something small for something huge." Now, 17 years later, the Whitsundays region has some of the best protection in the world for migrating humpback whales. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Galápagos corals show El Niño events are more extreme now than in past 1,000 years
item.description: Temperatures have warmed dramatically across the equatorial Pacific Ocean in 2026, signaling the onset of a strong and potentially historic El Niño. These events can affect weather around the world, and the intensity of recent El Niño events is raising alarm that, as global temperatures rise, they are becoming stronger and more destructive. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earlier swathing opens a new pathway for subterranean clover seed harvest
item.description: Subterranean clover's ability to bury its seed supports pasture persistence but makes commercial seed harvesting difficult. The industry relies on aging Horwood-Bagshaw (HB) suction harvesters, which collect seed from fully dry crops after repeated tillage and raking. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Awards First Prize in Phase 2 of Agency’s LunaRecycle Challenge
item.description: NASA named a team from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) as the first prize winner for Phase 2 of the agency’s LunaRecycle Challenge, which focused on developing solutions for reducing waste during missions to the Moon or deep space by recycling common materials, like fabrics, plastics, foam, and metals. The Composites for Extraterrestrial Recycling By Engineering the Reuse and Upcycling of Zotek (CERBERUZ) team, comprised of undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral students at MIT, received a total of $775,000 in awards. The technology grinds mixed trash into a fine powder, […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Bailey G. Light

item.title: Diverse portfolio of protected areas key to Mexican conservation efforts
item.description: In 2020, Mexico joined 150 nations committing to protect 30% of its territory by 2030 as part of the global 30x30 initiative. More than halfway through the decade, there is ongoing debate about how to effectively expand protected areas to meet that ambitious goal. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Low temperature graphene growth opens a route to sustainable resource recycling
item.description: Graphene is an exceptionally useful material for creating batteries, catalysts and electronic devices. Yet producing graphene typically requires temperatures as high as 900°C (1,652°F), limiting energy efficiency and making structural control difficult. To make graphene production more practical, a recent study has overcome this long-standing temperature barrier. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: US President Donald Trump on Friday announced the creation of a “Space Academy” to train future civilian and military recruits for an arena where the United States faces rivalry with China. Speaking at Nasa’s Johnson Space Centre in Houston, Trump said the institution would be modelled on the famed US military academy at West Point. “It’s called the US Space Academy. That’s a big deal,” Trump said as he signed an executive order creating the new school. “It’ll serve both the United States Space... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Dog-friendly dining isn't just a trend, it's good for business, new research shows
item.description: Restaurants that go beyond simply allowing dogs on patios by offering dedicated menu items for them can significantly boost customer traffic, spending and word-of-mouth, according to new research from Toronto Metropolitan University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fast fashion's carbon footprint can be reduced across its life cycle, new study suggests
item.description: Fast fashion is built on cheap, short-lived garments, especially cotton and polyester T-shirts. To sustain its profits, the industry relies on high production frequency, short product lifespan and a globalized supply chain. All these elements contribute to making the industry a major source of global pollution. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists capture first molecular-level images of water reorganization during a reaction crucial for life
item.description: Some of nature's most important chemical reactions rely on the coupled movement of negatively and positively charged particles. These processes play central roles in photosynthesis, catalysis and biological energy conversion yet remain difficult to observe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Honey bees can serve as sentinels for environmental health
item.description: Honey bees (Apis mellifera) are widely known as essential pollinators, but researchers using a "One Health" approach have also identified them as biological sentinels of environmental health. Honey bees continuously interact with their surrounding environment through the collection of nectar, pollen and water and can therefore be exposed to contaminants present in agricultural and natural ecosystems. Their health may consequently provide valuable information about environmental pressures affecting biodiversity and ecosystem functioning. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Breathable smart sensor developed for real-time hazardous gas detection on masks
item.description: A research team led by Sungwon Lee, a professor in the Department of Physics and Chemistry at DGIST, developed a hierarchical nano-on-nano structure by directly growing graphene nanowalls (GNWs) on polymer nanofibers and successfully used the structure to enhance the sensing performance of wearable gas sensors. The technology is expected to be applied to next-generation wearable sensors for real-time monitoring of individuals' breathing environments or hazardous gases in industrial settings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Motorboat noise stunts growth and impairs predator escape in reef fish, study shows
item.description: Coral reef fish that are exposed to motorboat noise grow up smaller and less able to dodge predators, new research shows. Scientists played either boat noise or natural reef sounds to a species from the Great Barrier Reef called the spiny chromis, both as embryos and soon after hatching. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: El pájaro que se extinguió por un cataclismo y la evolución decidió "fabricar" de nuevo milenios después
item.description: La historia de la vida en la Tierra está llena de grandes adaptaciones a las nuevas condiciones que se iban presentando, pero pocas son tan sorprendentes como la del rascón de Aldabra. Un ave endémica del atolón de Aldabra en las Seychelles que es protagonista de uno de los fenómenos más raros documentados en la biología evolutiva. Un estudio de 2019 sacó a la luz una prueba fósil que sin duda dejó a muchos sorprendidos. Hacemos referencia a un registro temporal que demuestra cómo un mismo linaje de aves colonizó una isla, evolucionó hasta perder el vuelo, se extinguió por completo tras un… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Joro spiders eat wider range of insects than Georgia's native orb weavers
item.description: When Joro spiders first arrived stateside more than a decade ago, scientists worried the massive black-and-yellow spiders would gorge themselves on the same bugs as native spiders (or even the native spiders themselves). If the invasive arachnids did make massive meals of Georgia's insects, the local orb weaver population—already facing dangers from insecticide and pesticide use—could suffer. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Less buying power, elevated inflation push down consumer views
item.description: Consumer sentiment dropped about 6% from last month, landing around 11% below a year ago amid continued worries that inflation will remain elevated for the foreseeable future, according to the University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Widespread use of AI tools could make it harder to craft effective business communications
item.description: Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT make it easier for business owners to produce polished pitches, business plans and other communications, but according to new research from The University of Manchester and Canada's University of Alberta, their widespread use could ultimately make it harder for businesses to effectively communicate with their audiences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mercury's crust points to deeper, hotter volcanic origins than expected
item.description: The evolutionary histories of Earth and Mercury differ fundamentally. The smallest planet, closest to the sun, likely began cooling early on, much like a setting pudding: As early as about 1 billion years after its formation, Mercury's volcanic activity came to a halt, and a solid, continuous "rock skin" formed on the planet's surface. Earth's crust, on the other hand, is still in motion: Volcanism and plate tectonics are constantly stirring up the "Earth pudding." Exactly what Mercury's unique volcanic past looked like and how it shaped its current appearance remain unclear. However… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nano-antennas make living cells light up brighter and faster
item.description: Researchers at Delft University of Technology have demonstrated for the first time that nano-antennas can enhance the fluorescence of proteins in living human and other mammalian cells. Scientists already use smart fluorescent proteins that light up when the electrical voltage across a nerve cell changes. By placing nano-antennas close to these light-emitting proteins, researchers can monitor processes inside cells with much greater precision. The discovery adds a new tool for revealing electrical signals in the brain through nanotechnology as well as genetic engineering. The research has… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A Google-like search engine for single-cell RNA data could answer previously impossible questions
item.description: Imagine doctors could understand exactly which cells caused a patient's cancer or whether pathogens contributed to the disease. They could then use the information to tailor a treatment plan to the patient's specific cancer. But answering such questions would mean wading through data from thousands of experiments locked in massive databases around the globe. Moreover, the search would take at least several days. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Once a legend, humpback whales make a comeback in Brazil
item.description: Female humpback whales off the coast of Brazil now have their pick of mates, who slap the water with their tails and jostle for attention—a scene that would have been unthinkable a few decades ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tracks and tooth marks reveal bone-crushing dogs at Nebraska supervolcano ashfall site
item.description: Thirty-five years on—well, 12 million, technically—Ashfall Fossil Beds State Historical Park continues to offer important glimpses of prehistoric life in Nebraska. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How methylation sets a parasite in motion to invade host cells
item.description: Parasites such as Toxoplasma gondii and the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum depend on rapid, precisely controlled movement to complete their life cycles. To start moving, they must assemble actin filaments at their front end and connect them to the molecular machinery that generates force. How these events are coordinated has remained unclear. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Self-blinking 'fairy lights' allow DNA to be imaged at almost double-helix-width resolution
item.description: Researchers have developed fluorescent molecules that permit imaging of how DNA is packaged inside living cells at unprecedented resolution and, in preserved cells, at a resolution close to the width of the double helix itself. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Diamond clock combines two signals to cut temperature-driven drift
item.description: Despite all the advertisements for engagement rings and necklace gifts, natural diamonds are imperfect. Their carbon atoms are arranged in a cubic lattice, but they nonetheless contain several types of crystallographic defects due to impurities that occasionally replace a carbon atom. The most common types of impurities are nitrogen and boron; "Type I" diamonds contain nitrogen impurities, which can be isolated or clustered, at concentrations of up to 1%, and make up about 95% of all natural diamonds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Experimental eye drops help blind mice see again
item.description: Scientists have created light-activated drugs that helped blind mice perceive light again and restored visually guided behavior without gene therapy, implants, or specialized lighting. Even more intriguingly, two of the most promising compounds worked when administered as eye drops, pointing toward a potentially simple new approach to restoring vision. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: We've reconstructed Melbourne's 200-year-old forests
item.description: Have you ever wondered what your Melbourne suburb looked like before all the streets and houses? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Engineered bacteria offer a new way to accelerate rock weathering for carbon removal
item.description: Rock weathering, the breakdown and dissolving of rocks and minerals caused by their exposure to water, air and biological life, is a major regulator of Earth's atmospheric CO2 levels and climate. Throughout Earth's history, rock weathering has been faster during warm periods with increased atmospheric CO2 levels. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Giving shorebirds space on the beach makes a big difference
item.description: When Ashley Dayer was walking on the beach with her 8-year-old son recently, he stopped her before she got too close to a group of shorebirds. "Momma, stop. We have to walk around the shorebirds," he told her. Dayer smiled. That moment was the perfect example of the human behavior change she and conservation partners have spent more than a decade trying to encourage along beaches used by both people and imperiled shorebirds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Roman telescope will see 100 times more sky than Hubble
item.description: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope will combine Hubble-like detail with a field of view 100 times larger, giving astronomers a sweeping new way to explore the cosmos. Its observations could uncover hidden planets, map billions of cosmic objects, and help scientists unravel the mysteries of dark matter and dark energy. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Bumblebees may self-medicate when exposed to fungal infections
item.description: There is an old saying that nature is the best medicine, and it turns out bumblebees might agree. A new study published in the journal Royal Society Open Science suggests that buff-tailed bumblebees (Bombus terrestris) may self-medicate when exposed to a fungal brood disease. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Kicking goals for junior sport culture
item.description: New research on improving behavior in youth sports calls for a move beyond trying to fix individual parents' and coaches' behavior to instead address the sporting culture in which behavior is learned, reinforced and normalized. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Compound with the potential to treat drug-resistant HIV identified
item.description: A large international team has developed a new compound that showed strong antiviral activity against HIV, including some drug-resistant variants. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Week in images: 24-28 August 2026 Discover our week through the lens Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Chimpanzees have been hurling rocks at the same trees for more than a decade
item.description: Some chimpanzees in West Africa repeatedly throw rocks at particular trees, creating piles of stones that can remain in use for more than a decade. Researchers think this unusual behavior may be cultural and could serve as a form of communication, territorial signaling, or something more symbolic. Camera traps and audio recordings are now being used to reveal who throws the stones and how nearby chimpanzees respond. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A common vape flavoring may disrupt early embryo development
item.description: A popular vanilla flavoring in e-cigarettes may interfere with some of the earliest steps of human development. In lab experiments, vanillin caused embryonic stem cells to lose their ability to develop normally and pushed them toward forming only certain types of tissue. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Ariane 6 launch with MTG-I2 – highlights
item.description: Video: 00:04:28 The Meteosat Third Generation -Imager2 (MTG-I2) satellite, has been launched on board an Ariane 6 launcher from Europe’s Spaceport in French Guiana. Liftoff was on 27 August 2026 at 22:11 CEST (17:10 local time). MTG-I2 is part of the MTG constellation for Eumetsat – two are already in orbit – and it will produce images for weather forecasting in Europe in unprecedented detail. This mission provides completely new data products and capabilities for European weather services, especially suited to nowcasting of severe weather events. The MTG-Imager satellites carry two… Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Researchers followed 400,000 kids for 20 years and found a lasting pre-K advantage
item.description: A 20-year study of 400,000 students found that children who attended public school pre-K earned better grades and test scores through high school than those in other childcare settings. Better-trained teachers and earlier exposure to structured classrooms may help explain why the advantage lasted so long. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Observing Samba and Tango’s reentries
item.description: The final two of ESA's pioneering Cluster spacecraft, Samba and Tango, will end their journeys as they burn up in our atmosphere on 31 August and 1 September respectively. Their targeted reentries mark the end of a mission that has transformed our understanding of Earth's magnetic environment. The final moments also offer a rare scientific opportunity for reentry observations from a plane. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based meat alternatives. Every one contained fungal toxins
item.description: Every one of 212 plant-based meat alternatives and drinks tested in the UK contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, though concentrations remained below recommended EU guideline levels. Researchers say the bigger question is whether regularly eating large amounts of these foods could lead to potentially concerning cumulative exposure over time. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: DR Congo begins Ebola vaccinations as deadliest outbreak on record spreads
item.description: Authorities are therefore using Ervebo under a compassionate-use programme while researchers gather data on whether it can protect against the current strain. Fuente: Africanews.

item.title: Elon Musk's rocket heads home to US after Christmas Island sojourn
item.description: The Starship 40 rocket that landed in the Indian Ocean and was towed to Christmas Island is finally heading back to the US after amusing locals for the past week. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: Scientists tracked 4,500 animals and found a surprising human effect
item.description: Scientists tracking thousands of animals found that our physical presence can reshape where wildlife moves and lives, sometimes as strongly as roads, cities, and other human development. Because different species reacted in very different ways, conservation efforts may need to become much more targeted. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: China’s commercial space sector expands global footprint with Thailand deal
item.description: Beijing-based GalaxySpace’s deployment this week of what it called China’s first turnkey satellite export to Southeast Asia underscores how the country is boosting its space influence overseas amid competition with Elon Musk’s SpaceX. GalaxySpace said it launched the Lingzhi-09 Thailand CubeSat aboard a Long March-6C rocket – alongside six other satellites – from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Centre in Shanxi province on Tuesday. Developed for Thailand’s Geo-Informatics and Space Technology... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Ben Jiang

item.title: Why scientists asked 1,000 people to bury their underwear
item.description: More than 1,000 volunteers buried cotton underwear across Switzerland to help scientists measure how active different soils are. The faster the fabric disappeared, the more biological activity was taking place underground. Gardens showed the fastest decomposition, while lawns had the least, revealing how strongly land management can shape soil life. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Low oxygen could limit insects' uphill escape from climate warming
item.description: Reduced oxygen levels and air pressure at higher elevations may limit insects' ability to move upslope to escape a warming climate, with potential consequences for the essential services they provide, like pollination, according to a new review in the journal, Functional Ecology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists find a huge hidden ice reservoir beneath Utah’s mountains
item.description: Beneath the rocky slopes of Mount Timpanogos lies far more ice than anyone walking across the surface might suspect. Researchers used gravity measurements to map the buried glacier in 3D and found it is about 83% ice, with enough frozen water to fill 600 Olympic swimming pools. Their findings suggest rock glaciers form as falling debris buries persistent snow and preserves it for thousands of years. Similar formations around the world may collectively store tens of gigatons of hidden water. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: People with more mobility in the labor market experience less discrimination
item.description: Employees who can easily change jobs are less likely to experience workplace discrimination. When dealing with a discriminatory employer, job mobility acts as an important incentive: If you can leave more easily, your employer will often make greater efforts to combat discrimination and retain you. That's what André van Hoorn writes in Economic and Industrial Democracy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Videos capture humpback whales stopping to snack as they migrate along Australia's coast
item.description: The southern humpback whale migration is in full swing. Tens of thousands of whales are now making their journey from warm Australian waters in the north to their cold feeding grounds in Antarctica. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Mad honey' that can stop your heart is now being sold online worldwide
item.description: A few months ago, a friend of mine told me that his father-in-law had been rushed to the hospital after eating some wild honey brought back from the hills of Nepal. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What employers are looking for in the age of AI — and four ways to provide it
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-01913-x For applicants whose knowledge of AI stops at the name ChatGPT, Nature spoke to academics, employers and early-career researchers to find out what you need to expand your understanding. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Hitting bacteria hard and early with diverse phage cocktails may curb resistance
item.description: As multidrug antibiotic resistance emerges as a potent public health challenge, medical science has renewed attention on the potential for bacteriophage therapy. Bacteriophages, or phages, are viruses that target, infect and replicate inside bacteria, destroying them in the process. To help maximize the success rate of this approach, researchers recently modeled the dynamics of bacteriophage therapy to explain particular therapies and optimize the composition of bacteriophage cocktails. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Evolution favors flatter paths when fitness outcomes are equal, study finds
item.description: A surprising discovery by Technion researchers sheds new light on the dynamics of evolution. Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study shows that when an organism has several evolutionary paths available with equal fitness, the path it follows is not necessarily chosen at random. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny oxygen gaps may determine whether next-generation memory films store data well
item.description: Researchers have captured in real time the "birth moment" when the performance of a next-generation memory material is determined. The key lies in controlling oxygen vacancies, microscopic defects created when oxygen atoms are missing from their normal positions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Boosting soybean protein: Zinc and sulfur essential in sustainable crop production
item.description: Soybean is a critical element of the global food supply: Between its use for animal feed and human consumption, it accounts for roughly two-thirds of plant-based protein meal output worldwide. Canada is a global leader in sustainable soybean production, with 70% of its crop, one of the country's top three by value, exported annually. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Primed and ready to fight, a nematode pheromone arms plants to battle pathogens
item.description: When cold and flu season comes around, we take steps like getting our flu shots and taking immune supplements to strengthen our bodies' defenses against pathogens. Plants face pathogenic threats, too. Plant pathogens can have devastating effects on crop yields, with up to 40% of global food crops lost annually, and such losses have severe implications for food security. But what if we could boost plant immune systems as we do our own and make them better able to withstand or fend off biological threats? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Vehicle-mounted spectroscopy system detects methane in real time
item.description: Researchers have developed a vehicle-mounted spectroscopy system that can reliably detect methane in real time while driving. Using a moving vehicle to detect methane could make it easier to locate hidden methane emissions across large areas. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Specific cover crops may help attract insects that target harmful pests
item.description: Different cover crops may affect how plants defend themselves against pests—including by attracting more insects that eat harmful caterpillars—according to a new study led by researchers at Penn State's College of Agricultural Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Discovery reveals rapid pathways to complex aromatic molecules in space
item.description: A team of researchers led by the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa Department of Chemistry has uncovered a faster way large carbon-based molecules may form in space, helping solve a long-standing mystery about how some of the building blocks of the universe grow. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Molecular makeover brightens organic light near 1,000 nanometers
item.description: Near-infrared organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) that emit about 1,000 nanometers could support biomedical and security technologies. Yet pushing organic light to these longer wavelengths usually causes a steep drop in efficiency. As the energy gap becomes smaller, molecular vibrations more readily turn excited-state energy into heat rather than light. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study reveals inter-city collaboration on emission reduction boosts sustainability performance
item.description: With Hong Kong recently recording record-breaking high temperatures, extreme weather has once again raised public awareness of global warming and emission-reduction measures. A large-scale international study led by The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) has revealed that intercity collaboration on emission reduction can improve overall sustainability performance by more than 10%. This comprehensive analysis covers 4,116 cities and spans 11 years of data, shedding new light on regional and global strategies for achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI model designs potentially stable protein sequences beyond those found in nature
item.description: A protein's function is determined by its structure, and structure—the way a protein folds—is determined by its sequence of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Short, intense storms gain intensity across Hawaiʻi
item.description: While long-term data show that Hawaiʻi is getting drier overall, short, intense downpours that cause sudden, dangerous flash floods are getting stronger on the islands, according to a new study by researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Shear flow in narrow channels sparks amyloid formation, experiments reveal
item.description: Many cars and not enough lanes is a recipe for traffic jams. Now, researchers from Japan show that even proteins can get backed up and start behaving poorly when too many try to squeeze too quickly through a small space. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Heat-tolerant corals may be more vulnerable to disease
item.description: Corals that partner with heat-tolerant algae may be better equipped to survive warming oceans—but that resilience comes with an unexpected trade-off, according to a new study from Boston University published in Science Advances. Fuente: Phys.org.
